source.title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
source.authors: Sangmin Bae; Yujin Kim; Reza Bayat; Sungnyun Kim; Jiyoun Ha; Tal Schuster; Adam Fisch; Hrayr Harutyunyan; Ziwei Ji; Aaron C. Courville; SeYoung Yun

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own isoFLOP and compute-optimal scaling analyses for a new architecture, Mixture-of-Recursions, and measures how parameter-sharing choices affect validation loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-loss comparisons across model sizes and compute budgets, but does not test whether those curves follow power laws or whether small-run fits extrapolate to much larger runs. Few-shot accuracy results are comparisons, not tests of downstream predictability. Rows below cover the compute-optimal allocation analysis and fixed-parameter comparisons of parameter-sharing architectures. Router, caching, and throughput results do not test the claim.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own isoFLOP grid (4 base sizes × 3 budgets) and fits curves to locate compute-optimal sizes for vanilla, recursive and MoR models. It also compares weight-sharing layouts at matched unique parameter counts. These results bear on V7 (the compute-optimal split depends on setup, here architecture) and on V4 (architecture details at fixed parameter count). It reports no power-law fits, no exponents and no extrapolation, so V1, V2 and V3 proper are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it leaves out the main conclusion. The authors conclude that MoR forms a new Pareto frontier: at equal FLOPs it has lower validation loss and better few-shot accuracy than vanilla and recursive baselines, with fewer parameters and higher throughput. They also find that MoR's compute-optimal path favours larger models trained for fewer tokens. Middle-Cycle is 'consistently the safest' sharing choice, though Cycle is slightly ahead at 135M with Nr=2.
record.recipe_differences: Uses isoFLOP validation-loss analysis and fits polynomial functions to compare compute-optimal paths, but studies MoR and recursive architectures rather than fitting the original scaling-law setup; it uses FineWeb-Edu and a trapezoid schedule with checkpoint reuse.
record.method_sensitivity: Compute-optimal allocation differs by architecture. Validation NLL among parameter-sharing strategies varies with base scale and recursion count.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed 118M unique params and 10B tokens, more recursions lower validation NLL (2.9678, 2.9205, 2.9111 for Nr=1,2,3; Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss improves with added compute via weight reuse at fixed unique parameter count.

record.problems: The compute-optimal analysis reports no numerical path points or fitted exponents in the text, and the plotted data are figure-only. Training used checkpoint reuse with a trapezoid schedule for isoFLOP comparisons. The study is limited to models up to 1.7 billion parameters and one dataset.
record.rows_left_out: None; all extracted rows are included.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss in parameters, tokens or compute. Table 9 has only 3 budgets per size.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fitted exponents for optimal N or D versus compute, and no token-count optimum. Stability of the power is untested.
No variation of depth/width aspect ratio in untied transformers.
Text pretraining only. The uptraining in Table 12 is not a scaling-form test.
Few-shot accuracy is reported but not modelled as a function of scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, schedules or datasets.

missing.what: IsoFLOP NLL grid underlying Fig. 5a, e.g. MoR 360M: 3.1026, 2.9161, 2.7924 at 2, 5, 16.5e18 FLOPs
Vanilla reduced-size baselines at 10B tokens (e.g. 315M 2.8471, 157M 2.8908, 98M 2.9449), needed to scale the sharing-order gaps
At 1.7B and 68.5e18 FLOPs vanilla beats MoR; authors attribute this possibly to differing optimal token counts

record.verdict_notes: This is an architecture paper whose scaling content is secondary. V3 links were removed from r1–r3 because no exponents are fitted; those rows now bear on V7 only. The V4 rows are read as equal-parameter pairs, since a single NLL value cannot show a shape effect. Pairs across Cycle and Middle variants differ in unique params and are confounded. Whether sharing order in tied models falls inside V4's 'wide range' is debatable, hence limits_scope rather than challenges.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or tests of loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits are used to predict the loss of larger runs.
The paper reports a compute-optimal path for MoR, but not fitted power exponents or separate parameter-count and token-count scaling laws.
Tests parameter-sharing schemes at matched unique parameter counts; does not systematically vary depth, width, or a wide range of conventional architecture details.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling tests.
Reports few-shot accuracy, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The analysis shows architecture-dependent compute-optimal behavior, but does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, schedules, or datasets to establish their separate effects.
